title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs

details.title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
details.abstract: LOWN (Look Only When Needed) is a training-free decoding method for diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) that processes the image only when a text-only prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Diffusion VLMs such as LLaDA-V process the whole image at every denoising step, but we find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs and cuts generation time by 57.4% on average. Project page: https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/ Code: https://github.com/hyeon9698/LOWN

Given a single input — a document page, a natural image, a chart / flowchart, a geometry figure, an audio clip or an audio-visual video — it produces one structured JSON envelope that covers both perception (layout elements, text, tables, formulas, bounding boxes, timestamps, ASR, OCR, acoustic events, camera motion) and cognition (captions, narratives, reports). details.title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
details.abstract: We introduce SpecSlot, a role-coupled tokenization method for pixel-space generative Transformers. SpecSlot decouples fine visual detail from global communication by assigning tokens fixed spectral output roles: low-frequency carriers perform global attention, while the remaining slots interact locally. On ImageNet-512, SpecSlot-K4 uses 38.2% fewer FLOPs than JiT-B/16. For 256×256 text-to-image generation, it reduces forward compute from 218.77 to 129.86 GFLOPs while improving DPG-Bench from 61.15 to 62.21. details.title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training
details.abstract: Excited to share WorkFactory, a scalable framework for synthesizing coherent and executable professional tasks to train Working Agents! WorkFactory combines professional intent synthesis, information support graphs, and execution-guided repair to construct high-quality tasks that enable reliable expert demonstrations. We build 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and train the WorkPilot model family at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales. All three models achieve consistent improvements across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B improving from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. We hope this work contributes to scaling general-purpose agents for real-world professional tasks!

title: A Broader Look into MLLM's Retrieval Heads

details.title: A Broader Look into MLLM's Retrieval Heads
details.abstract: We study how omni-modal LLMs retrieve relevant evidence, focusing on how retrieval mechanisms extend from text and vision to audio-visual inputs. Across 18 model checkpoints, including eight omni-modal models, we find that retrieval relies on a sparse set of attention heads that are largely preserved from language or vision-language backbones. By presenting the same evidence as speech or on-screen text, we show that audio and visual retrieval largely recruit the same heads. Ablating the shared subset, comprising fewer than 2% of all attention heads, also degrades document understanding, spatial perception, and visual mathematics, revealing its role in broader multimodal capabilities. Building on these findings, we optimize retrieval-head attention with a ranking objective for document retrieval, improving Qwen3-VL-8B’s page Recall@1 on MMDocIR by 6.03 percentage points over the untrained scorer, with gains across three model families.

title: Intrinsic Distribution Matching

details.title: Intrinsic Distribution Matching
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We’re excited to share IDM: Intrinsic Distribution Matching . Can a generator provide both the score supervision and the representation used for distribution matching? Building on internal DMD, IDM retains the full DMD correction and adds an explicit loss on the means and per-coordinate standard deviations of the generator’s own EMA features , without an external feature encoder. A Gaussian-plus-residual decomposition of the reverse-KL field motivates this additional moment constraint. At 2 NFE , IDM (Z-Image) achieves 94.25% on LongText-CN and 90.20% on LongText-EN , the best scores among the compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show consistent gains from the added moment loss, while generator EMA features perform competitively with DINOv2. We evaluate both Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B with full-parameter and LoRA tuning. Model weights: coming soon. title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models

details.title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models
details.abstract: Can a coding agent turn a real user's multimodal request into a complete, working application revision? We're sharing Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models , a benchmark built around real users' requests to revise existing applications. Each task starts with a runnable application and asks the agent to understand the user's intent, make the necessary changes, and satisfy every acceptance criterion. Real requests, multimodal inputs, and connected changes. Co-Design Bench contains 273 tasks and 2,331 expert-authored acceptance criteria , curated from 37,463 deduplicated queries across 26,314 real user coding sessions . It covers two complementary tracks: Multimodal Editing (100 tasks): localized revisions grounded in annotated screenshots and optional image, audio, video, or document inputs. Repository Editing (173 tasks): coordinated changes across components, routes, state, data flow, and content. Requests can involve reproducing distinct text animations from a video, correcting a dashboard from a receipt and updating its dependent totals, or coordinating layout and interaction changes across an application. Tasks span Grounded Understanding, UI Transformation, and Functional Implementation , often combining several capabilities within one request. Evaluate the running application, with evidence for each requirement. Our reference-free judge-then-refute protocol assesses hidden acceptance criteria using source code and browser evidence. A separate verifier challenges positive judgments for stubs, hardcoded outputs, unreachable functionality, and requirement mismatches. Evidence audits require screenshots for visual claims and recorded browser actions for interaction claims. No gold implementation or target screenshot is required. Partial requirement satisfaction and complete delivery tell different stories. Across 10 model endpoints under a shared agentic harness , the strongest endpoint, gpt-6-astra , passes an average of 69.9% of criteria per task , yet fully satisfies only 26.4% of tasks . All ten endpoints achieve lower criterion completion on repository requests spanning three or four edit types than on those spanning one or two. Qwen3.8-27B reaches 64.4% overall strict completion , ranking fourth overall, and 64.5% on Repository Editing , ranking second on that track in this evaluation. It also leads the text-only Multimodal Editing subset at 77.9% . Rankings vary with the editing setting; the small repository-track score differences do not establish a general model advantage. The ME-96 subset comprises 96 Multimodal Editing tasks and 521 acceptance criteria , a distinct scope from the full 273-task paper evaluation. Explore the real cases, demonstrations, evaluation tools, and results: Project & demos · Paper · Code & evaluation · Dataset We welcome researchers and builders working on coding agents, multimodal grounding, and reliable application editing to try the benchmark and share their findings!

title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?

details.title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?
details.abstract: Evaluating forecasting capability usually means waiting for outcomes to materialize — months, sometimes years — during which market conditions, fundamentals, and the information environment shift enough that scores can no longer be cleanly attributed to the model; moreover, most work in LLM4Finance has focused on the research stage rather than the investment stage, which is where the field's core objective lies. ILE asks whether an agent, using only what was visible at decision time, can independently complete the full chain from evidence to assumptions to forecast. To answer it, we built a versioned corpus (3.43M document versions, 1.52TB, 9 source classes) that enforces the cutoff across the entire toolchain — specify a timestamp and you get exactly the versions visible at that moment — and organized 86 assignments around buy-side analyst deliverables, with rubrics anchored to sources and reproducible calculations through financial dependency graphs. Among current SOTA systems, Astra scores 78.9 on Research & Evidence but only 52.5 on Forecast & Model, and ordering by realized outcomes puts DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ahead (40.3 vs 37.7): today's models are very good at organizing evidence of what has already happened into coherent analysis, and not yet good at turning that analysis into judgment about what has not. For me, the longer-term significance is on the training side — once the time boundary is a mechanism, historical timestamps become a re-samplable environment for large-scale domain RL, with evaluation and training sharing one environment.

title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker

details.title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
details.abstract: Glance: one model. Judge, rank, generate. RAG usually serves two models: a cross-encoder reranker that encodes every (query, passage) pair, then a generator that reads the winners again. We show the generator can be its own reranker. All k passages are prefilled once into a shared state, one short probe per passage continues from that cache, and a LoRA + pointer head scores every passage in the same pass. With the adapter off, the same weights chat as usual. On a 9B hybrid (Gated DeltaNet) backbone: 39 min of training on one B200: SciFact nDCG@10 0.741, NFCorpus 0.345 (bge-reranker-v2-m3: 0.721 / 0.326) Scales to k=200 candidates: 0.717 vs 0.659 for BGE (SciFact subset) HotpotQA answer F1 +0.045 over BGE-selected context, same generator (paired bootstrap CI excludes 0) Activated variant: chat stays bit-identical to the base model, and the answer continues the reranking cache Adapters + code (Apache-2.0): https://huggingface.co/airun-ai/GlanceRAG-MiMo-9B-Reranker

title: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding

details.title: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding
details.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.

title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps

details.title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps
details.abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.

title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm

details.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
details.abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training

details.title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training
details.abstract: Weight-normalized (WN) training is emerging as a compelling alternative to conventional weight decay (WD), with recent studies reporting substantial pretraining loss gains. We show that these gains are driven primarily by the induced effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory rather than by normalization alone. Matching ELR trajectories largely collapses the training loss dynamics of WN and WD. Schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal learning rate (LR) alone. Building on this principle, we propose AIR ( A ffine I nverse-square- R oot decay), which combines a theoretically derived $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay with an affine adjustment to satisfy prescribed peak and terminal LRs over a finite training horizon. We further identify late-stage ELR scheduling as a key source of its gains, because a shared late schedule attenuates the effect of earlier LR choices. Experiments on 128 B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining demonstrate that AIR outperforms cosine and other candidate schedules in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative LR. Applying the same ELR trajectory to WD reproduces the corresponding training dynamics, showing that the benefits extend beyond fixed-norm training and establishing ELR as the principled scheduling object.

title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification

details.title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification
details.abstract: We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement. The same tasks can also be used to benchmark other provers and as rewards for reinforcement learning.

title: Unlocking Any-Order Generation in Pretrained Autoregressive Image Models

details.title: Unlocking Any-Order Generation in Pretrained Autoregressive Image Models
details.abstract: Many AI image generators build a picture one piece at a time, always in the same order: left to right, top to bottom, like reading a page. Because of this fixed habit, they cannot fill a missing patch in the middle of a photo, extend an image beyond its borders, or redraw one region while keeping the rest. Existing alternatives are trained from scratch, at roughly three times the computing cost. We show that existing generators can instead learn to work in any order with brief extra training. Two ideas make this possible: the model is told which spot it will fill next, and training shifts gradually from the familiar order to random ones, so the model keeps what it already knows. The adapted models fill, extend, and edit images competitively, with a small loss in everyday image quality, letting today's models gain new skills without being rebuilt.

title: After One-Click Video: The Inflow of Service-Type Content, the Failure of the Recommendation Pool Mechanism, and the BoLe System

details.title: After One-Click Video: The Inflow of Service-Type Content, the Failure of the Recommendation Pool Mechanism, and the BoLe System
details.abstract: One-click video tools now let anyone make good-looking content fast. Most of it is service-type content: people watch it to meet a need, not to enjoy the content itself. Before competing, creators, tool builders and model researchers should first ask which kind they are making, because the two kinds win by different rules. Our paper draws this line, and uses a simple model to show why the free platform’s trial-viewing pool stops working when service-type content keeps pouring in. Try the demo: set AI output to 100x and watch one year.

title: FDSML: Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning with Parameter-Aware Triplet Loss

details.title: FDSML: Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning with Parameter-Aware Triplet Loss
details.abstract: FDSML pre-trains vision models without real images, using the generating formula itself as supervision: fractals with more similar parameters should lie closer in the embedding space. We turn this parameter-space ordering into triplets, so the model learns how images relate to each other.

title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?

details.title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?
details.abstract: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study conditional interaction, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching $1/\rho_u$, where $\rho_u$ is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: $\rho_u$ is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.

title: R^2Orch: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Orchestration via Self-Play within a Skill-Internalization Loop

details.title: R^2Orch: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Orchestration via Self-Play within a Skill-Internalization Loop
details.abstract: R²Orch (Recursive Self-Play Orchestration) trains an agent orchestrator without a hand-designed curriculum: an inner self-play loop improves the orchestrator on tasks a Proposer picks, and an outer loop improves how that inner loop learns. The Proposer is rewarded for tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn (Recursive Learnability), and each skill is withdrawn once self-play shows the orchestrator does as well without it (Skill Withdrawal), moving it toward zero-skill deployment. Tested with zero skills, a 9B orchestrator is best on all twelve benchmarks across QA, math, code, and interactive tasks, raising the average over the strongest baseline from 86.0 to 89.8 in distribution and from 76.1 to 78.8 out of distribution (AIME 2026: 74.0 → 81.3). Code: https://github.com/beita6969/R2Orch Model: https://huggingface.co/beita6969/R2Orch-9b

title: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems

details.title: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems
details.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts, and guides their updates according to their respective roles. This structure allows shared coordination rules to be refined consistently across agents while keeping execution instructions separately adjustable. CEPO provides the prompt structure and optimization guidance, while existing prompt optimizers perform the underlying search. Extensive experiments spanning 11 benchmarks across four domains demonstrate that applying CEPO to four existing prompt optimizers consistently improves their performance. Ablations and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, while controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents.

title: HiFOR: Hierarchical Foresight with Action-Guided World Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Model

details.title: HiFOR: Hierarchical Foresight with Action-Guided World Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Model
details.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore, Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

title: FrameForge: Harnessing Priors of Video Foundation Models for Unified Image Generation

details.title: FrameForge: Harnessing Priors of Video Foundation Models for Unified Image Generation
details.abstract: Unified conditional image generation requires a single model to preserve different aspects of a visual input while producing a target image that follows textual guidance. Pretrained video models provide a promising foundation by encoding visual transformations across time, yet existing approaches typically assign the condition and target to fixed temporal positions. We observe that condition-target relationships vary substantially across generation tasks, while video models naturally encode visual transformations at different temporal scales. This motivates us to model conditional generation through input-adaptive virtual temporal relations. We propose FrameForge, which captures two complementary aspects of such relations. Mixture of Temporal Experts (MoTE) models how far the target lies from the condition by dynamically selecting temporal RoPE experts with different virtual intervals. Chain of Temporal Reasoning (CoTR) models how the condition is transformed into the target through a latent intermediate state, with a reasoning-bottleneck attention mask encouraging information propagation through this pathway. Experiments on DreamBench, COCO2017, and GEdit-Bench show that FrameForge achieves superior performance in subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and image editing among the compared methods.

title: Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control

details.title: Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control
details.abstract: 🪄 Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control! Existing game world models produce realistic visuals but remain constrained by familiar environments and predefined motions. Control largely focuses on locomotion, with limited support for articulated actions. Can a world model follow an unseen character swinging a sword, spreading its wings, or transforming mid-battle? Wizard decouples character animation, scene manipulation, and gameplay logic from visual generation. Agents control articulated skeletons and scene geometry through structured visual proxies, while explicit world states support adaptive boss behavior and mechanics-consistent combat. We construct 50.3 hours of aligned proxy–video pairs spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters. Character-aware adaptive masking preserves reference appearance, while causal adaptation and few-step distillation enable interaction at 24 FPS, with zero-shot generalization to unseen scenes, characters, and motions. From world exploration and character summoning to transformation and scene manipulation, Wizard gives players greater freedom to create and control their own game worlds. Code coming soon!

These agents develop their own control routines. Most converge on a dynamic split between the VLA policy and code-as-policy, and nearly all build a persistent memory across episodes. title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents

details.title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
details.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-aspolicy (CaP) puts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet, existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that brings this recipe to CaP and turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. Within this harness, we first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, and then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL, however, must credit tens of requests from the agent, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode. Since training runs in simulation, we introduce a physical critic that reads the privileged physical state in simulator, which the policy never sees, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B achieves 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning

details.title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: We split the training-inference mismatch in LLM RL into a numerical discrepancy, which stays nearly constant, and a policy lag, which compounds through the trainer's own updates. From this split we derive the discrepancy-lag correction (DLC), which keeps stale-sampler training within the noise of on-policy runs.

title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search

details.title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
details.abstract: Personalization should clarify user intent, not overwrite it. How can we build a compact query rewriter that understands users' personalized intent while avoiding intent drift? We introduce WeFair , a fidelity-aware alignment framework for personalized query rewriting in short-video search. The key idea is to align different types of human feedback with different stages of training: Demonstration (SFT): Learn from large-scale search-session data and real user reformulations. Preference (DPO): Capture user preferences from subsequent consumption behavior. Verification (GRPO): Use exact human reformulations and preservation targets to enforce intent fidelity. One of our key findings is that richer behavioral rewards do not necessarily lead to more faithful rewriting. Strict, verifiable human feedback proves more effective for preventing intent drift during on-policy optimization. Results are encouraging: WeFair-2B outperforms strong baselines in offline overall accuracy and intent preservation. Online A/B testing achieves a +2.593% relative lift in effective video-view rate and a 2.350% relative reduction in query reformulation rate . The model is deployed in WeChat short-video search, serving 100M+ queries per day . We hope this work offers useful insights into building efficient, reliable, and intent-faithful language models for real-world search systems. 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16927v2

title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation

details.title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
details.abstract: We introduce Wave Forcing, a training and execution framework for streaming video generation. The key idea is wavefront scheduling: later video chunks begin denoising before earlier chunks finish, using their cleaner intermediate states as causal context. WaveRT sends K/V ahead of use and overlaps communication with computation. After pipeline fill, each concurrent forward round produces one video chunk. Key results: • Quality: On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing. For 100-second videos, Dynamic Degree improves from 36.63 to 91.45 and Subject Preservation from 92.75 to 97.10. • System efficiency: Our 4-step benchmark on 8×H200 reaches 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS, delivering 7.07× single-GPU E2E throughput.å • Parallelism: Up to 2.53× the throughput of the faster Ulysses/Ring baseline in DiT-only tests with  matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, step counts and GPU counts. Code, training recipes, and 4-step/5-step checkpoints are available. We welcome feedback and discussion! title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement

details.title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement
details.abstract: Video generation is evolving from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic systems that integrate planning, tool use, and feedback. Meanwhile, video world models are enabling interactive, action-conditioned environments for agents. In this survey, we explore their intersection through the lens of the  agent harness , an executable runtime that manages tools, context, state, feedback, and budgets around video models. We focus on three areas: Agentic Video Generation: Multi-shot planning, production, editing, and evaluation. Agentic World Modeling: Interactive observation, control, and state management. Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI): Improving video outputs, harnesses, models, and the improvement process itself. We also discuss essential agent capabilities and open challenges toward autonomous video production and self-improving video systems. 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40191 🌐 Homepage: https://agentic-videogen.github.io/ 💻 Github: https://github.com/agentic-videogen/awesome-agentic-videogen

title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models

details.title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
details.abstract: We introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for robot-use agents with open-weight models, designed to support further training. Without privileged inputs, out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, exceeding the published GPT-6 Astra–RoboProbe result of 28.97, while also performing competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Beyond benchmarking, we systematically analyze models across generations, families, and sizes, identifying four general capabilities linked to effective robot use. Our findings suggest that future robot-use agent training should develop these capabilities jointly.

title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings

details.title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
details.abstract: Despite shared mathematical foundations, embedding research across text, vision, audio, graphs, tables, and time series remains largely fragmented into modality-specific silos. This survey and position paper argues that embedding research is quietly converging around universal principles: contrastive learning objectives, Transformer backbones, the pretrain–finetune recipe, and an upward shift toward whole semantic units. To evaluate progress toward true unification, we introduce the 3C framework—Coverage, Comparability, and Compositionality—which maps onto three progressive paths: format transformation, cross-modal alignment, and deep joint fusion, our advocated terminus that subsumes alignment and eliminates the modality gap. Reaching this goal will require preserving unique modality-specific structures, cross-pollinating techniques across research communities, and building unified benchmarks that measure true compositional gains.

title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers

details.title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
details.abstract: DeFT-RAG asks a different question about multi-hop RAG: instead of planning all sub-questions and their dependencies in advance, what if the LLM writes just one self-contained sub-question at a time? Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, so it never has to be rewritten, and its answer stays correct for any question that asks it. The rest of the work moves outside the LLM: a QA table updated by rules keeps track of what is known, and a fine-tuned 4B decision model makes the yes/no decisions and estimates question depth. A QA cache reuses answers across questions. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among 13 baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6, including +5.2 points on MuSiQue over Hi-Q, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a shared QA cache, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, reducing LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy. 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37826 💻 Code: https://github.com/Dingyi-Kang/DeFT-RAG 🤗 Decision model: https://huggingface.co/Dingy-Kang/DeFT-RAG-DM-4B

title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers

details.title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers
details.abstract: Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19-23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running 24.5× faster on TREC DL and 16.7× faster on BRIGHT.

title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads

details.title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
details.abstract: Multi-agent collaboration fundamentally reshapes LLM serving workloads through dynamic dependencies, synchronization, and context sharing—beyond what conventional request-level benchmarks can capture. We introduce MAServeBench , a benchmark featuring composable hierarchical collaboration patterns and dependency-preserving Semantic Traces for reproducible serving evaluation and architecture simulation. Our GPU/NPU studies reveal how collaboration affects compute efficiency, KV cache pressure, and end-to-end task performance. We hope this work helps guide the design of next-generation serving systems and hardware for agentic AI. Feedback and discussions are very welcome!

title: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Teacher Evolution

details.title: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Teacher Evolution
details.abstract: We wanted to solve a frustrating problem in On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD): the "self-teacher" model often gets blinded by the privileged context and gives pretty unreliable, overconfident token-level guidance, which ends up misleading the student model. To fix this, we proposed TESD (Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation): We let the teacher evolve dynamically by optimizing it with environment feedback. We automatically down-weight those training samples where the teacher's guidance is deemed unreliable. As a result, TESD consistently beats standard token-level distillation (like SDPO) and even sequence-level RL (like GRPO) across benchmarks like SciKnowEval and Tooluse.

title: Behind Video Generation: Observations and Insights on Multimodal Understanding from Kling

details.title: Behind Video Generation: Observations and Insights on Multimodal Understanding from Kling
details.abstract: This technical report shares practical lessons from the evolution of Kling’s video-generation systems. It argues that the next bottleneck is no longer visual rendering, but semantic control—the ability to understand what to generate, preserve, organize, and evaluate. Centered on Kling-MLLM, the report examines the full data–conditioning–alignment–evaluation pipeline, covering dense and reference-grounded captioning, prompt enhancement, perceptually grounded text encoders, reward models, and task-specific evaluation. It offers a valuable system-level perspective on how multimodal understanding enables more controllable, coherent, and production-ready video generation.

title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild

details.title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild
details.abstract: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four embodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, though all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and π0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement across embodiment-specific task suites (Kendall’s W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance after fine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all three embodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.

We introduce MoviEdit , an end-to-end framework for scalable long-form multi-shot video editing that jointly addresses the challenges of (1) data , (2) modeling , and (3) evaluation . title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified

details.title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
details.abstract: Introducing Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified. Learn to reason: model-aware construction of challenging, self-contained scientific problems. Learn to investigate: verifiable tasks that require retrieving information and using tools. title: Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems

details.title: Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems
details.abstract: When a foundation model moves into a new domain, there's usually little expert-written data or reliable supervision to train on. Recursa adapts to the domain by learning from its own experience, without human experts or a stronger teacher model. A knowledge repository stores what the system learns: domain-specific skills, instructions on when to use them, memories of past tasks, and reflections on what to improve. Bootstrapping: the system builds the repository from domain materials and practices on tasks it generates from them. This targets the knowledge gap. Recursive self-improvement: parallel learners run tasks and propose local improvements, which are validated and merged back into the repository. This targets the behavior gap. The system's own model drives the whole process, including improving how it learns. On Harvey LAB's Firm Knowledge benchmark, Recursa raises the all-pass rate on held-out test tasks from 30.0% to 55.0% with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and from 35.0% to 46.0% with Qwen3.8-Flash. title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations

details.title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
details.abstract: PrimeSim is an action-conditioned, multiview world model that runs as a robot simulator. It starts from a pretrained video generator, midtrains on 30,110 hours across 22 platforms, then posttrains into a causal few-step generator. Posttraining combines self-rollout training, so the model learns from its own generated histories rather than only real frames, with a selected KV-cache memory that carries context across chunks. Inference runs at over 10 FPS with all three camera views. PrimeSim scores first overall on EWMBench and leads four of five WorldSimProbe suites against state-of-the-art baselines. Rollouts stay coherent over long horizons and transfer to held-out platforms within 100-200 gradient steps. We also use the model as an environment for reinforcement learning: GRPO post-training inside PrimeSim raises LIBERO success from 61.7% to 73.2%, and the model's success predictions track the physics simulator closely enough to rank policies. All experiments are in simulation (AgiBot G2, LIBERO, RoboTwin); no physical robot is used, and closed-loop hardware deployment is future work. Weights and code will be released on the 6th of November. Project page: https://primebottech.github.io/PrimeSim-website/

title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories

details.title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories
details.abstract: Do AI reviewers recognize the improvements authors make through revision? We introduce PaperTrajectory-2026, covering 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations along 14 revision dimensions. Evaluating eight AI reviewers, we find that most revisions annotated as major improvements receive unchanged scores, with weak agreement across reviewers on the direction of score changes. Even when revisions earn higher scores, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage. Our study highlights the need for AI reviewers whose judgments track substantive improvements and remain stable when the scientific evidence is unchanged.

title: "Shall We Approve?" Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents

details.title: "Shall We Approve?" Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents
details.abstract: Does a coding agent really know what its next command will do? Approving every command by hand does not scale: Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts anyway. So agents now rely on automated approvers, such as Claude Code's Auto Mode, rule-based checkers, and guardrail models. All of them judge the text of the command. Yet a command's behavior is decided by the scripts it invokes and the workspace it runs in, and the same command can be harmless in one project and destructive in another. We propose Caper , which approves a command after seeing what it does. Each command is pre-executed in a snapshotted sandbox under system-call tracing. An LLM approver reviews a compact report of the observed effects: file changes, network attempts, and reads of secrets. Allowed commands are committed; blocked ones are rolled back, and the agent gets a reason it can act on. Compared with six existing systems, Caper has the lowest harmful-outcome rate on SABER (6.7% vs. at least 14.8%) and on YoloFS-Ext, our benchmark that hides harm inside the tools agents are asked to run (7.8% vs. at least 35.3%). It blocks only 1.0% of the safe twins. Code and data: https://github.com/wudaoz/Caper

title: Is Forgetting Unified? Exploring Concept Unlearning in Unified Multimodal Models

details.title: Is Forgetting Unified? Exploring Concept Unlearning in Unified Multimodal Models
details.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks require agents to learn, reason, and generalize robustly across complex real-world environments. However, existing approaches often struggle with partial observability, fragmented spatial reasoning, and inefficient integration of heterogeneous memories, limiting their capacity for long-horizon adaptation. To address this, we introduce RoboMemory, a brain-inspired framework that unifies Temporal, Spatial, Semantic, and Episodic memory for efficient long-horizon planning and interactive learning. Its core innovations are a comprehensive memory system designed for embodied tasks, and a dynamic spatial knowledge graph for scalable, consistent memory updates. Extensive experiments on EmbodiedBench show that RoboMemory improves the average success rate of Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Ins by 26.5 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to strong closed-source VLM agents. Real-world trials further suggest RoboMemory's potential for interactive environmental learning by reusing accumulated experience across repeated task attempts. These results demonstrate RoboMemory as a scalable memory-augmented framework for embodied agents, improving long-horizon planning and cumulative learning in complex interactive environments.

title: Where to Learn and How Far to Roll Out: Efficient Adaptive Training for GUI Agents

details.title: Where to Learn and How Far to Roll Out: Efficient Adaptive Training for GUI Agents
details.abstract: Trajectory-level GRPO is a common approach for training multi-step GUI agents, but repeatedly rolling out complete trajectories from the task root can be inefficient: task-level rewards provide coarse supervision over which intermediate decisions require improvement, while already-mastered prefixes are repeatedly re-executed before reaching difficult states. We introduce a two-stage adaptive training framework that jointly addresses where to learn and how far to roll out. We first construct reusable intermediate checkpoints from successful expert trajectories and select informative pivots using action disagreement, which measures uncertainty directly from sampled GUI actions. Stage I performs one-step RL at these pivots to improve uncertain local decisions. Stage II then progressively expands policy responsibility through adaptive Local, Suffix, and Root training according to task progress. Recoverable checkpoints enable repeated training from intermediate states without replaying the preceding trajectory. Across MobileGym and CUA-Gym-Hub, our method reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to Vanilla GRPO while improving task performance, demonstrating that jointly allocating training across states and rollout ranges can substantially improve GUI-agent RL efficiency.

title: SeMo3D: Unifying 3D Generation, Editing, and Completion via Selective Modeling

details.title: SeMo3D: Unifying 3D Generation, Editing, and Completion via Selective Modeling
details.abstract: 3D generation, editing, and completion are typically treated as regenerating the complete 3D asset under task-specific constraints, even when only a local region needs modification. This leads to task isolation, inconsistency in content that should remain unchanged, and dependence on task-specific paired data. We address these issues with a key observation: the three tasks all synthesize a designated region while keeping the rest intact---the full region for generation, the target region for editing, and the missing region for completion. We term this paradigm Selective Modeling and build SeMo3D upon it; it naturally unifies the three tasks, preserves unchanged content by construction, and enables training without paired editing or completion data, since any 3D asset can be partitioned into a selected region and its context. For training, we propose region-selective denoising, which randomly selects regions of varying sizes on standard 3D assets and applies noise and loss only to them, jointly learning all three tasks. For architecture, we propose Omni3DiT, a multi-condition 3D diffusion transformer that distinguishes regions to create from those to retain and fuses image, text, and point guidance for fine-grained control. Experiments across three benchmarks show SeMo3D surpasses state-of-the-art methods on all tasks, delivering multimodal controllability in generation and strong consistency and accuracy in editing and completion. SeMo3D further serves as a unified modeling tool for agents, enabling efficient 3D creation through natural-language interaction. Project page: https://xiaokunsun.github.io/SeMo3D.github.io Code: https://github.com/XiaokunSun/SeMo3D

It introduces the tilted novice, a low-rank input-dependent replacement for pruned experts, which improves over MoNE’s constant replacement with only ~1.2–1.8% additional parameters, while showing that no single replacement operator universally dominates.

The results reveal distinct strengths across models: similar spatial scores can accompany very different planning success, and achieving early subgoals does not ensure completion of a full task sequence. title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data

details.title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
details.abstract: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs $21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus $5 for a render contract; every further episode costs $0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs $107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of $117 for teleoperation in China and below $290 in labour alone in North America.

title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies

details.title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
details.abstract: NEO-VLA challenges a common assumption in VLA design: that action should rely on visual representations distilled for semantic understanding. Our findings suggest that effective control instead benefits from early visual computation. Native representations transfer well to action even when frozen, while exposing intermediate features in encoder-based VLMs does not yield comparable gains. This highlights the importance of how visual representations are formed, rather than encoder removal alone. Moreover, NEO-VLA shows strong robustness to visual shifts but remains challenged by changes in spatial configurations and task goals. Together, these findings suggest that the next frontier of embodied intelligence lies in bridging perception and flexible control, motivating native representations that are intrinsically action-relevant.

title: StreamDuo: A Live Commentator and a Research Agent for Unseen Games

details.title: StreamDuo: A Live Commentator and a Research Agent for Unseen Games
details.abstract: 🎮 Can a live AI commentator handle a game it has never seen before? We introduce StreamDuo , a two-agent framework for cross-game streaming commentary. Instead of relying solely on memorized game knowledge, a live commentator selectively queries a frozen research agent that retrieves relevant information from game wikis, all while the stream continues. Our key contributions include: Information-gain-based querying to learn when external knowledge is actually needed. On-policy self-distillation to help the commentator use noisy retrieved information effectively. Cross-game evaluation on 10 unseen games after training on only Baldur's Gate 3. StreamDuo improves entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 and reduces source-game knowledge leakage from 9.9% to 1.0% compared with the retrained Proact-VL baseline, while achieving stronger commentary timing and quality. Beyond real or fake , the same weights also tell you where a recording was synthesized, which system made it, whether two recordings share a source , what the channel did to it, and why , in short lines you can check against the audio. 🥇 #1 open-weight on Speech-DF-Arena (2.14% EER over 14 test sets) and on SpoofRadar v1.0 (4.04%) 🔍 The decision follows the evidence: edit the stated synthesized span and the decision flips 🎯 Catches 99.6% of partially edited recordings with reasoning (vs 78.4% answering in one step) ⚡ 2.9B parameters, runs on a single 12 GB GPU; only 29.7M parameters are trained 🤗 VeriSpoof-Plus · VeriSpoof-Base · Demo · VeriSpoof-Bench Happy to answer questions!

title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding

details.title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding
details.abstract: Excited to share SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding! On-policy supervision does not have to wait for full-response rollouts. SpecOPD samples fresh draft branches at reference anchors in parallel, shares target-prefix computation, and supervises each branch on its own sampled history. An E2E-TV surrogate directly targets acceptance length. Algorithm–system co-design makes this work across full, sparse, and linear attention: tree masks, branch-consistent indexer groups, and indexed state replay preserve branch histories while reusing shared computation. Results: Up to 41.45% higher five-benchmark mean acceptance length than the original drafter. 16.09× supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD with the 27B target and DFlash V2 under native configurations, excluding offline reference preparation. Up to 3.56× decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding on the 27B target. We evaluate Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.8-27B, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-125B with DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2 across dialogue, coding, math, and agentic workloads. The repository currently contains the project overview and figures; training code, evaluation scripts, and model weights are not included in the initial release. Feedback and discussions are welcome!

title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation

details.title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation
details.abstract: Few-step distillation seeks to make diffusion and flow models efficient without sacrificing generation quality. While score-based distribution matching methods provide a strong foundation, accurately tracking the student's evolving distribution across intermediate few-step transitions remains challenging: direct score estimation on perturbed intermediate outputs suffers from high variance, whereas clean-target denoising can estimate a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Building on a flow-matching perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), a unified framework that constructs student velocity fields along the sampling process and uses a learned critic to turn student–teacher velocity discrepancies into generator feedback. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and conditional moment matching along two axes (which field to match and how to update the generator).

details.abstract: Evaluating models on full benchmarks is often expensive. Benchmark compression reduces this cost by using small subsets to approximate full-benchmark results. This paper theoretically explains why random sampling works surprisingly well for benchmark compression but can be unstable, and introduces BestRand, a simple, stable, and low-cost solution. Across 70+ benchmarks, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4%, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost of competing methods.

title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex

details.title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
details.abstract: We present Drex, a family of four open decision models that return a calibrated probability distribution over user-defined options in a single forward pass, without autoregressive decoding. Each request pairs a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) with questions asking for a choice, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. The family spans 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B-A3B (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with our in-house RL recipe, reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), which blends verified outcomes with a reasoning judge under a KL constraint; ablations show RLAF raises accuracy while consistency losses cut option-order flips from 6.3% to 4.2%. Drex Max sets a new state of the art among decision models on Decision Index 0.4.1 (67.52 vs. 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0) and holds its score on maintainer-run private tests (66.60). On the independently run Artificial Analysis Decision Index, Max has the second-highest score among decision models, and Drex is among the most widely used decision models on OpenRouter. It contains 204 human-written tasks across five search categories, spanning 7 domains and 25 subdomains. The tasks require agents to connect information across images, objects, and search steps to compare candidates, follow visual clues, and produce complete answers. details.title: Open-HumanScale: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models

We study how human experience can improve robot learning, using Open-HumanWAM-50K , a 50,000-hour egocentric corpus with hand-motion and language annotations. 📈 HumanWAM-Vanilla — scaling human experience: our exploration studies show that scaling egocentric pretraining improves generalization to unseen scenes and randomized environments. Greater data diversity strengthens the scaling trend, while human pretraining improves robot demonstration efficiency. The final model achieves 92.08% Clean / 68.88% Random , averaging 80.48% on RoboTwin 2.0 . 🤖 HumanWAM-Goal — zero-shot transfer: combining human and robot experience improves zero-shot generalization in simulation and the real world. Visual goals enable robots to follow human demonstrations and adapt their behavior through in-context conditioning, without target-task parameter updates. 🏆 RoboTwin 2.0 Rank #1: after post-training, HumanWAM-Goal achieves 92.70% Clean / 84.60% Random , averaging 88.65% . title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training

details.title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training
details.abstract: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of a base execution system through sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness. Directional Harness Evolution develops specialized sibling harnesses along distinct repair directions, forming a reusable Sibling Harness Pool that remains fixed during policy training. Complementary Harness Rescue Training invokes this pool only when all initial attempts under the base harness fail. The same policy generates fresh rollouts under selected auxiliary harnesses, and these trajectories replace the failed group for reinforcement learning. An Adaptive Harness Router selects the Top-k variants using Harness Behavior Profiles and voting across multiple LLMs. Policy-aware profile re-anchoring refreshes this evidence as the policy learns. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness. Behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy itself. Reusing the router for Rank-1 inference provides additional gains at the same executor rollout count.

title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma

details.title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
details.abstract: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.
